## Overview

Every diffusion model so far in this book samples $p(x)$. This chapter asks
for $p(x \mid c)$: a super-resolved image given a low-resolution one, a
picture given a caption, a face given a reference. The lecture gives two
routes, and the chapter follows the same division. **Conditional training**
puts the condition into the network and learns $\nabla\log p(x_t \mid c)$
from paired data; it is what SR3, Stable Diffusion and every text-to-image
system does, and it costs a training run for each kind of condition.
**Guidance** leaves a pretrained unconditional model untouched and injects
the condition into the sampler instead --- through the initial point
(SDEdit) or at every step (ILVR) --- which buys one model for many tasks at
the price of sampling from something that is not quite the posterior.

Nothing in the machinery changes. The sampler is still @eq-ddim-step, the
network still predicts noise, and the manifolds of
[Why Diffusion Models](ch08.qmd) still have to be hit in the right
order. What changes is which score the sampler is given. The chapter ends
with a two-dimensional example in which every score is known in closed form,
so each claim --- that conditional training learns the conditional score,
that ILVR satisfies its constraint exactly, that SDEdit is posterior
sampling --- is checked against an exact answer rather than against a
trained network.

## Where unconditional generation stood

@fig-unconditional puts three models side by side before the conditioning
begins: StyleGAN2-ADA [@karras2020ada], DDPM [@ho2020] and the reverse SDE
[@sde]. By 2020 the two diffusion constructions had caught up with the best
GAN on unconditional image synthesis, which is what makes the question of this
lecture worth asking: conditioning a model is only interesting once the
model itself is good enough that the conditioned samples are worth looking
at. The rest of the lecture never returns to GANs.

The point of the slide is that the two diffusion models are no longer behind the GAN. ## Conditional training {#sec-cond-train}

We now want samples from $p(x \mid c)$ for a condition
$c$. A sampler needs only the target's score at every level (@thm-reverse), here $\nabla_{x_t}\log p(x_t \mid c)$.
Bayes' rule, with $p(c)$ independent of $x_t$, splits it:

$$
\nabla_{x_t}\log p(x_t \mid c)
= \nabla_{x_t}\log p(x_t) + \nabla_{x_t}\log p(c \mid x_t) .
$$ {#eq-bayes-score}

**Conditional training** (this section) learns the left side directly from
paired data $(x_0, c)$ by giving $c$ to the
network. **Guidance** (@sec-guidance) keeps an unconditional model for the
first term on the right and supplies the second at sampling time.

### SR3: super-resolution by conditional training

In SR3 [@saharia2022sr3] the condition is a low-resolution image
$x$ and the target a high-resolution image $y$. In this
subsection $y_t$ is the image chain ($y_0$ clean,
$y_T \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$), $\gamma_t$ plays
the role of $\bar\alpha_t$ and $f_\theta$ is the noise predictor. The
forward chain is the VP process on $y$; the reverse chain
$p_\theta(y_{t-1} \mid y_t, x)$ sees the
condition at every step.

**Training (Algorithm 1).** Draw $(x, y_0) \sim p(x, y)$,
$\gamma \sim p(\gamma)$ and $\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$,
and take a gradient step on
$\Vert f_\theta(x, \sqrt{\gamma}\,y_0 + \sqrt{1 - \gamma}\,\epsilon, \gamma) - \epsilon \Vert_p^p$,
$p \in \{1, 2\}$.

**Inference (Algorithm 2).** From $y_T \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$,
for $t = T, \dots, 1$,

$$
y_{t-1} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}}\left( y_t - \frac{1 - \alpha_t}{\sqrt{1 - \gamma_t}}\, f_\theta(x, y_t, \gamma_t) \right) + \sqrt{1 - \alpha_t}\,z,
\qquad z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I) \ (z = 0 \text{ at } t = 1) .
$$ {#eq-sr3-step}

![SR3 as the lecture draws it on slides 58-59. Above, the chain runs on the target $y$ while the low-resolution $x$ is held fixed, so the forward kernel is the ordinary $q(y_t\mid y_{t-1})$ and only the reverse kernel $p_\theta(y_{t-1}\mid y_t,x)$ sees the condition. Below, Algorithm 1 trains $f_\theta$ on the noise it must subtract and Algorithm 2 is the DDPM step with $f_\theta(x,y_t,\gamma_t)$ in place of $\epsilon_\theta$. Reproduced from the slides [@lecture-slides-diffusion; @saharia2022sr3].](figures/lec08/dodoyou0125-sr3-algorithms.png){#fig-sr3 width=100%}

Three points are left implicit in @fig-sr3.

**(i) The loss learns the conditional score.** For $p = 2$, the argument of
@eq-bayes-optimal conditioned on $x$ makes the minimiser
$\mathbb{E}[\epsilon \mid y_\gamma, x]$, and
@thm-tweedie with the prior $p(y_0 \mid x)$ (valid because
the noise is independent of $(x, y_0)$) gives

$$
f^\star(x, y_\gamma, \gamma) = -\sqrt{1 - \gamma}\;\nabla_{y_\gamma}\log p(y_\gamma \mid x) ,
$$ {#eq-cond-score}

the left side of @eq-bayes-score; nothing else in the machinery changes.
(For $p = 1$ the minimiser is a conditional median, not exactly a score.)

**(ii) Noise-level conditioning.** SR3 feeds the network $\gamma$ itself,
drawn from a continuous range during training, so the same network serves
any inference schedule. This is the time-embedding mechanism of @fig-unet-time with $\gamma$ in place
of $t$.

**(iii) Algorithm 2 is the DDPM step.** With $y \to x$,
$\gamma_t = \bar\alpha_t$ and $f_\theta \to \epsilon_\theta$,
the posterior mean of @prp-ddim-marginal is
$\frac{\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}(1 - \alpha_t)}{1 - \bar\alpha_t}x_0 + \frac{\sqrt{\alpha_t}(1 - \bar\alpha_{t-1})}{1 - \bar\alpha_t}x_t$.
Substituting the Tweedie estimate
$x_0 \approx (x_t - \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_t}\,\epsilon_\theta)/\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}$,
the coefficient of $x_t$ is

$$
\frac{1}{1 - \bar\alpha_t}\left( \frac{1 - \alpha_t}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}} + \sqrt{\alpha_t}(1 - \bar\alpha_{t-1}) \right)
= \frac{1 - \alpha_t + \alpha_t - \bar\alpha_t}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}\,(1 - \bar\alpha_t)}
= \frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}},
$$

and that of $\epsilon_\theta$ is
$-(1 - \alpha_t)/(\sqrt{\alpha_t}\sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_t})$: the mean of
@eq-sr3-step. The only difference from @eq-ddim-step with $\eta = 1$ is the
noise variance, $1 - \alpha_t$ instead of $\tilde\beta_t^2 \le 1 - \alpha_t$;
both are standard choices in @ho2020.

**How the condition enters.** SR3 upsamples $x$ bicubically and
concatenates it with $y_t$ along the channels, so the U-Net sees the
condition pixel-aligned. @fig-sr3-results shows what comes out: a blurred
low-resolution input, the SR3 output and the reference. The output is sharp
because each step denoises towards a *sample* of $p(y \mid x)$ rather than
regressing to its blurry mean, and the lecture's demonstration runs the same
model from $64 \times 64$ to $1024 \times 1024$.

![SR3 results as the lecture shows them: the low-resolution input, SR3's output and the reference, for a face and for a flower. The output is not the blurry conditional mean that a regression loss would give, because each reverse step samples. Taken from the lecture slides [@lecture-slides-diffusion], after @saharia2022sr3.](figures/lec08/slide58-sr3-results.png){#fig-sr3-results width=70%}

### Latent diffusion with a text condition

Pixel-space diffusion at high resolution is expensive, and a text prompt is
not pixel-aligned. Latent diffusion [@rombach2022ldm], the model behind
Stable Diffusion, addresses both.

**Latent space.** A pretrained autoencoder maps an image
$x \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}$ to
$z = \mathcal{E}(x) \in \mathbb{R}^{h \times w \times c}$, with
downsampling factor $f = H/h$ and $\mathcal{D}(z) \approx x$.
Diffusion runs entirely on $z$, so each U-Net pass costs a factor $f^2$
fewer positions (64 for $f = 8$), and more for attention, which is quadratic
in the number of positions.

**Conditioning.** An encoder $\tau_\theta$ maps the condition (text, a
semantic map, an image) to $L$ tokens, $\tau_\theta(c) \in \mathbb{R}^{L \times d_\tau}$,
and the objective is the conditional noise-prediction loss on latents,
$\mathbb{E}\Vert \epsilon - \epsilon_\theta(z_t, t, \tau_\theta(c)) \Vert_2^2$
with $z_t = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,\mathcal{E}(x) + \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_t}\,\epsilon$,
whose minimiser is the conditional latent score by @eq-cond-score.

**Cross-attention.** A feature map is flattened into $hw$ tokens
$\varphi(z_t) \in \mathbb{R}^{hw \times d_\varphi}$, and each $QKV$ block
computes

$$
\operatorname{softmax}\!\left( \frac{Q K^\top}{\sqrt{d}} \right) V,
\qquad
Q = \varphi(z_t) W_Q, \quad K = \tau_\theta(c) W_K, \quad V = \tau_\theta(c) W_V .
$$

$Q$ has one row per image position and $K, V$ one per token, so after the
row-wise softmax $QK^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{hw \times L}$ gives every image
position a distribution over the tokens (*which words matter here*), and the
output is a weighted average of token values. Nothing depends on $L$ except
the size of the sums, so prompts of any length work and no spatial
alignment is needed. The "switch" in @fig-ldm picks the route: spatially
aligned conditions are concatenated with $z_t$ as in SR3, and sequences
such as text enter through cross-attention.

![The latent diffusion architecture of slide 61. The encoder $\mathcal{E}$ and decoder $\mathcal{D}$ move between pixel space and the latent space in which the diffusion runs; the conditioning encoder $\tau_\theta$ feeds the $QKV$ cross-attention blocks of the denoising U-Net, and the switch selects concatenation for spatially aligned conditions. Reproduced from the slides [@lecture-slides-diffusion; @rombach2022ldm].](figures/lec08/dodoyou0125-ldm-architecture.png){#fig-ldm width=95%}

### Text-conditioned training

The lecture states the text-conditioned loss in pictures: a cat image for
$x_0$, a noise image for $\epsilon$, and the word "Cat" as the condition.
With the time argument restored it is

$$
\Big\Vert \epsilon_\theta\big( \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_t}\,\epsilon, \, t, \, c \big) - \epsilon \Big\Vert_2^2 .
$$ {#eq-text-loss}

Its TL;DR, "Train a diffusion model to estimate noise only when noise is
added to a video along with the corresponding text", has two key words. The
target is *only noise*: the text is an input, never a target, so the model
denoises *knowing* the caption. And training needs the *corresponding* pairs
$(x_0, c)$, after which
$\epsilon_{\theta^\star}(x_t, t, c) = -\sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_t}\,\nabla\log p(x_t \mid c)$
by @eq-cond-score. The loss is written for an image, and the same recipe
with $x_0$ a video clip gives text-to-video. Sampling is
@eq-ddim-step with $\epsilon_\theta(x_t, t, c)$,
and every guarantee of the unconditional sampler carries over with
$p(x_0 \mid c)$ in place of $p_0$.

The lecture closes the section with what the recipe produces. **eDiff-I**
[@balaji2022ediffi] keeps the content of the prompt "A {X} photo / painting
of a penguin working as a fruit vendor in a tropical village" fixed while X
sets the style (@fig-ediff); it trains separate *expert* denoisers for
different ranges of $t$, which fits the shell picture of
[Why Diffusion Models](ch08.qmd), since the inputs at different levels live
on almost disjoint tubes. Midjourney, Stable Diffusion 2 and DALL-E 2
[@ramesh2022dalle2] differ in data, encoders and scale but not in the
principle of @eq-text-loss. **Sora** [@brooks2024sora] applies that
principle to video latents with a transformer, generating the walk down a
neon-lit Tokyo street of @fig-sora from a paragraph-long prompt.

![One prompt, six styles, from eDiff-I [@balaji2022ediffi]. Only the $X$ of "A {X} photo / painting of a penguin working as a fruit vendor in a tropical village" changes between the panels, and the penguin, the fruit and the village survive it: one network holds both what the scene contains and how it is rendered, and the caption decides each. Taken from the lecture slides [@lecture-slides-diffusion].](figures/lec08/slide64-ediff-styles.png){#fig-ediff width=85%}

![A frame of the Sora clip the lecture plays [@brooks2024sora], generated from a paragraph describing a woman walking down a neon-lit Tokyo street. The model is @eq-text-loss applied to video latents. Taken from the lecture slides [@lecture-slides-diffusion].](figures/lec08/slide66-sora.png){#fig-sora width=85%}

The price of conditional training is **paired data and a training run for
each kind of condition**: a super-resolution model cannot inpaint.
@sec-guidance removes this restriction by putting the condition into the
sampler instead of the network.

## Guidance-based approaches {#sec-guidance}

Guidance needs neither paired data nor retraining. It takes a pretrained
**unconditional** model, which supplies $\nabla\log p(x_t)$, and
injects the condition at sampling time: SDEdit through the *initialisation*,
ILVR at *every step* by replacing low frequencies, and inverse-problem
solvers at every step through the *likelihood* term of @eq-bayes-score. All
three sample, exactly or approximately, from a posterior with the diffusion
model as the prior.

### SDEdit: conditioning through the initial point

SDEdit [@meng2022sdedit] starts from a guide image $x^{g}$, such
as a crude stroke painting with the right layout but no realism, and uses no
condition-specific training. It **perturbs** the guide to an intermediate
level $t_0$ with @eq-forward-marginal,
$x_{t_0} = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t_0}}\,x^{g} + \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_{t_0}}\,\epsilon$,
and then **reverses** with the unconditional sampler @eq-ddim-step from
$t_0$ to $0$. (The paper writes this for the VE-SDE; the VP form is the same
idea.) In @fig-sdedit, natural images (green) and stroke paintings (blue) are
far apart at level $0$ but overlap after perturbation, so the noisy guide is
a typical point of the noisy image distribution, and the reverse process
carries it to the images: the merging of modes established in [Why Diffusion Models](ch08.qmd).

**What SDEdit samples.** Suppose the reverse chain is exact (the DDPM step
with $\theta^\star$ approximates it). The forward chain is Markov, so the
reverse transitions from $t_0$ compose to the law of $x_0$ given
$x_{t_0}$:

$$
p(x_0 \mid x_{t_0})
\;\propto\; q(x_{t_0} \mid x_0)\,p_0(x_0)
\;\propto\; \exp\left( -\frac{\bar\alpha_{t_0}}{2(1 - \bar\alpha_{t_0})}\,
\Big\Vert \frac{x_{t_0}}{\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t_0}}} - x_0 \Big\Vert^2 \right) p_0(x_0) .
$$ {#eq-sdedit-posterior}

Since $x_{t_0}/\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t_0}} = x^{g} + s_{t_0}\epsilon$,
SDEdit is posterior sampling with prior $p_0$ and a Gaussian likelihood
centred on the noisy guide, weighted by the signal-to-noise ratio
$\mathrm{SNR}(t_0) = \bar\alpha_{t_0}/(1 - \bar\alpha_{t_0})$. This makes
the lecture's trade-off exact: a small $t_0$ (high SNR) is **faithful** to the
guide but stays unrealistic if the guide is far from the data, and a large
$t_0$ is **realistic** but forgets the guide, becoming an unconditional
sample as $t_0 \to T$. @fig-sdedit-examples collects the lecture's examples
--- stroke painting to image, image compositing, stroke-based editing ---
and all of them are this one algorithm; only the guide changes.

![SDEdit on slide 69. The stroke painting (left) is perturbed by the forward SDE until its law overlaps that of natural images, and the reverse SDE then carries it back down; the contours above the images are the distributions of photographs (green) and of strokes (blue), which meet only after the perturbation. Reproduced from the slides [@lecture-slides-diffusion; @meng2022sdedit].](figures/lec08/dodoyou0125-sdedit-overview.png){#fig-sdedit width=100%}

![The three tasks the lecture gives SDEdit, all with the same unconditional model and the same algorithm. Stroke painting to image (upper left), image compositing (lower left) and stroke-based editing (right); each group pairs the guide the user supplies with the sample the reverse chain returns. Taken from the lecture slides [@lecture-slides-diffusion], after @meng2022sdedit.](figures/lec08/slide70-sdedit-examples.png){#fig-sdedit-examples width=95%}

### ILVR: conditioning at every step

ILVR [@choi2021ilvr] conditions on a reference image $y$ through its
low frequencies ($x$ is again the image chain). With
$\phi = \phi_N$ a linear low-pass filter (downsample by $N$, upsample back),
one step is

$$
x'_{t-1} \sim p_\theta(x'_{t-1} \mid x_t), \qquad
y_{t-1} \sim q(y_{t-1} \mid y), \qquad
x_{t-1} = \phi(y_{t-1}) + (I - \phi)(x'_{t-1}) :
$$ {#eq-ilvr}

an unconditional proposal, the reference noised to the same level, and a
merge that keeps the proposal's high frequencies and the noisy reference's
low frequencies. @fig-ilvr-graphical is the lecture's drawing of one such
step. Three facts explain the step.

![One ILVR step. From $x_t$ the unconditional model proposes $x'_{t-1}$; the reference $y$ is noised to the same level as $y_{t-1}$; and the latent variable refinement replaces the low frequencies of the proposal by those of the noisy reference, giving $x_{t-1}$. Nothing in the model is retrained. Taken from the lecture slides [@lecture-slides-diffusion], after @choi2021ilvr.](figures/lec08/slide71-ilvr-graphical.png){#fig-ilvr-graphical width=95%}

**(i) The low frequencies are matched exactly.** If $\phi^2 = \phi$ --- for
example $N \times N$ block averaging $D$ followed by nearest-neighbour
upsampling $U$, where $DU = I$, and $\phi = UD$ is even an
orthogonal projection since $D = N^{-2}U^\top$ --- then
$\phi(x_{t-1}) = \phi^2(y_{t-1}) + (\phi - \phi^2)(x'_{t-1}) = \phi(y_{t-1})$.
At the last step the reference is almost noise-free, so
$\phi_N(x_0) \approx \phi_N(y)$.

**(ii) It is a projection onto the noisy constraint set.** For an orthogonal
projection $\phi$, the closest point to $x'$ in
$\{x : \phi x = \phi y_{t-1}\}$ is
$x' - \phi x' + \phi y_{t-1}$, which is
@eq-ilvr: a *hard* data-consistency step for the noise-free linear problem
$\mathcal{A} = \phi_N$.

**(iii) It stays on the right tube.** Both pieces carry noise of level
$t - 1$, so $x_{t-1}$ has the noise level the next network expects (the
noisy manifolds of [Why Diffusion Models](ch08.qmd)). Inserting the *clean* $\phi(y)$ instead would put
the input off $\mathcal{M}_{t-1}$.

$N$ controls how much is imposed, since the range of $\phi_N$ has dimension
$n/N^2$: small $N$ gives near copies of the reference, large $N$ fixes only
coarse layout and colour. @fig-ilvr shows this for
$N = 4, \dots, 64$, and the same algorithm for image translation,
paint-to-image and scribble editing.

![ILVR across the downsampling factor, from slide 72. (a) With $N=4$ the output is nearly the reference; by $N=64$ only the coarse layout and colour survive and the identity is gone, which is $\phi_N$ having range of dimension $n/N^2$. (b-d) The same algorithm as image translation, paint-to-image and scribble editing. Reproduced from the slides [@lecture-slides-diffusion; @choi2021ilvr].](figures/lec08/dodoyou0125-ilvr-results.png){#fig-ilvr width=100%}


### Inverse problems, in one paragraph

The same route reaches further than SDEdit and ILVR. An imaging system
$\mathcal{A}$ --- a camera, a microscope, an MRI scanner --- produces
$y = \mathcal{A}(x) + n$, and recovering $x$ is ill-posed, so a prior is
needed; a diffusion model is one. Writing the posterior score as

$$
\nabla_{x_t}\log p(x_t \mid y)
= \underbrace{\nabla_{x_t}\log p(x_t)}_{\text{pretrained network}}
+ \underbrace{\nabla_{x_t}\log p(y \mid x_t)}_{\text{measurement}}
$$ {#eq-posterior-score}

splits the work: the first term is the unconditional network through
@eq-epsilon-score-conversion, and the second is the hard part, because
$y$ and $x_t$ are conditionally independent given $x_0$, so
$p(y \mid x_t) = \int p(y \mid x_0)p(x_0 \mid x_t)\,dx_0$ involves the
intractable $p(x_0 \mid x_t)$. Diffusion posterior sampling
[@chung2023dps] approximates it by Tweedie's $\hat{x}_0$, and the
accelerated solvers [@chung2024dds] build on that. That material is the next
chapter, *Conditional Diffusion Models for Inverse Problems*; here
@eq-posterior-score is
needed only because the worked
example below samples the exact posterior to check the approximations
against.


![Guidance on a two-dimensional prior with the exact score. (a)
Unconditional samples lie on the crescent. (b, c) SDEdit from the guide
(star): a small $t_0$ is faithful but leaves the output short of the data, a
large $t_0$ is realistic but ignores the guide, the trade-off of
@eq-sdedit-posterior. (d) ILVR keeping the first coordinate pins
$x_1 = y_1$ (dashed line) and fills in $x_2$ from the prior. (e) Exact
posterior samples for the same constraint. 400 samples per
panel.](figures/lec08/Kwak-MJ-guidance-2d.png){#fig-guidance-2d width=100%}

## Worked example: conditional sampling with an exact score {#sec-example}

A trained network only approximates the score, and its errors would blur any
check. We therefore take data whose score is known *exactly* at every
level, a Gaussian mixture, replace the network by its ideal value
$\theta^\star$, and test the sampler @eq-ddim-step, conditional sampling
@eq-posterior-score, ILVR @eq-ilvr and SDEdit @eq-sdedit-posterior against
closed-form answers. The code needs only numpy; paste the blocks into one
Python session in order (a few seconds in total). It is the computation
behind @fig-guidance-2d.

### Three closed forms

Let $p_0 = \sum_{k=1}^{K} w_k\,\mathcal{N}(\mu_k, \Sigma_k)$
on $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ with positive definite $\Sigma_k$.

**(a) Noisy marginals.** Given component $k$, $x_t$ is a linear map
of independent Gaussians, so

$$
p_t(x) = \sum_{k} w_k\,\mathcal{N}\big(x;\, \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\mu_k,\, \bar\alpha_t\Sigma_k + (1 - \bar\alpha_t)I\big) .
$$ {#eq-gmm-noised}

**(b) Score.** For a mixture with terms $\mathcal{N}_k$ of means
$m_k$ and covariances $C_k$,
$\nabla\mathcal{N}_k = -\mathcal{N}_k\,C_k^{-1}(x - m_k)$, so

$$
\nabla_{x}\log p(x)
= -\sum_k r_k(x)\,C_k^{-1}(x - m_k),
\qquad
r_k(x) = \frac{w_k\mathcal{N}_k(x)}{\sum_j w_j\mathcal{N}_j(x)} ,
$$ {#eq-gmm-score}

with the responsibilities $r_k$ computed from logarithms to avoid
underflow. With @eq-gmm-noised and @eq-epsilon-score-conversion this gives the ideal
$\epsilon_{\theta^\star}^{(t)}$ at every level.

**(c) Linear-Gaussian conditioning.** For $y = Ax_0 + n$,
$n \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_{n}^2I)$,
component $k$ conditions to
$\mathcal{N}(\mu_k + G_k(y - A\mu_k), \Sigma_k - G_k A\Sigma_k)$
with $S_k = A\Sigma_k A^\top + \sigma_{n}^2I$
and $G_k = \Sigma_k A^\top S_k^{-1}$
($x_0 - G_ky$ is uncorrelated with, hence
independent of, $y$), and its weight becomes proportional to
$w_k\,\mathcal{N}(y; A\mu_k, S_k)$. So
$p(x_0 \mid y)$ is again a mixture. Since $x_t$
and $y$ are conditionally independent given $x_0$,
running the sampler on this posterior mixture uses the exact left side of
@eq-posterior-score. The SDEdit law @eq-sdedit-posterior is case (c) with
$A = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t_0}}\,I$,
$\sigma_{n}^2 = 1 - \bar\alpha_{t_0}$ and $y = x_{t_0}$.

### Step 1: the Gaussian shell

The Gaussian shell theorem of [Why Diffusion Models](ch08.qmd) predicts that $\Vert X\Vert/(\sigma\sqrt{n})$
has mean close to $1$ and standard deviation close to $1/\sqrt{2n}$.

```{.python}
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(618)

# (1) Gaussian shell: ||X|| / (sigma sqrt(n)), X ~ N(0, sigma^2 I_n)
sigma = 0.5
for n in [3, 100, 10_000]:
    X = sigma * rng.standard_normal((2000, n))
    r = np.linalg.norm(X, axis=1) / (sigma * np.sqrt(n))
    print(f"n = {n:6d}: mean {r.mean():.4f}, std {r.std():.4f}, "
          f"1/sqrt(2n) = {1 / np.sqrt(2 * n):.4f}")
```

Output:

```{.text}
n =      3: mean 0.9351, std 0.3963, 1/sqrt(2n) = 0.4082
n =    100: mean 0.9953, std 0.0704, 1/sqrt(2n) = 0.0707
n =  10000: mean 1.0002, std 0.0069, 1/sqrt(2n) = 0.0071
```

### Step 2: the prior and the exact sampler

The prior is the crescent of @fig-guidance-2d: $K = 7$ components on an arc
of radius $2.5$ centred at $(0, -1)$, with standard deviation $0.3$ along
the arc and about $0.063$ across it. `reverse` is @eq-ddim-step with the
ideal network, on a VP schedule with $T = 200$ and $\beta_t$ linear from
$10^{-4}$ to $0.06$ ($\bar\alpha_T \approx 2 \times 10^{-3}$). `report`
prints the mean and standard deviation of each coordinate and the mean
distance from the arc ("off-arc"), a measure of realism.

```{.python}
# (2) Prior: a thin crescent in R^2 built from K = 7 Gaussians.
ang = np.linspace(0.15 * np.pi, 0.85 * np.pi, 7)
tang = np.stack([-np.sin(ang), np.cos(ang)], 1)        # (K, 2) tangent
nrm = np.stack([np.cos(ang), np.sin(ang)], 1)          # (K, 2) normal
prior = (np.full(7, 1 / 7),                            # weights (K,)
         np.stack([2.5 * np.cos(ang), 2.5 * np.sin(ang) - 1], 1),
         0.09 * np.einsum("ki,kj->kij", tang, tang)    # covs (K, 2, 2)
         + 0.004 * np.einsum("ki,kj->kij", nrm, nrm))


def gmm_sample(B: int, gmm: tuple) -> np.ndarray:
    w, mu, cov = gmm
    k = rng.choice(len(w), B, p=w / w.sum())
    z = rng.standard_normal((B, mu.shape[1]))
    L = np.linalg.cholesky(cov)
    return mu[k] + np.einsum("bij,bj->bi", L[k], z)


def gmm_score(x: np.ndarray, gmm: tuple) -> np.ndarray:
    """grad_x log sum_k w_k N(x; mu_k, cov_k); x: (B, d)."""
    w, mu, cov = gmm
    diff = x[:, None, :] - mu[None]                    # (B, K, d)
    Pd = np.einsum("kij,bkj->bki", np.linalg.inv(cov), diff)
    logr = (np.log(w) - 0.5 * np.einsum("bki,bki->bk", diff, Pd)
            - 0.5 * np.linalg.slogdet(cov)[1])
    r = np.exp(logr - logr.max(1, keepdims=True))
    r /= r.sum(1, keepdims=True)                       # responsibilities
    return -np.einsum("bk,bki->bi", r, Pd)


def condition(gmm: tuple, A: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray,
              var: float) -> tuple:
    """Exact p(x | y) for y = A x + noise, noise ~ N(0, var I)."""
    w, mu, cov = gmm
    S = A @ cov @ A.T + var * np.eye(len(y))           # (K, m, m)
    Si = np.linalg.inv(S)
    G = cov @ A.T @ Si                                 # (K, d, m)
    res = y - mu @ A.T                                 # (K, m)
    logev = (np.log(w) - 0.5 * np.einsum("ki,kij,kj->k", res, Si, res)
             - 0.5 * np.linalg.slogdet(S)[1])
    wp = np.exp(logev - logev.max())
    mu_p = mu + np.einsum("kim,km->ki", G, res)
    return wp / wp.sum(), mu_p, cov - G @ A @ cov


# VP schedule; index 0 is the clean level (abar_0 = 1).
T = 200
alpha = 1 - np.r_[0.0, np.linspace(1e-4, 0.06, T)]
abar = np.cumprod(alpha)


def noised(gmm: tuple, ab: float) -> tuple:
    """Law of sqrt(ab) x_0 + sqrt(1 - ab) eps, x_0 ~ gmm."""
    w, mu, cov = gmm
    d = mu.shape[1]
    return w, np.sqrt(ab) * mu, ab * cov + (1 - ab) * np.eye(d)


def reverse(x: np.ndarray, t0: int, gmm: tuple, eta: float = 1.0,
            after_step=None) -> np.ndarray:
    """eq-ddim-step from level t0 down to 0, exact score of gmm."""
    for t in range(t0, 0, -1):
        s = gmm_score(x, noised(gmm, abar[t]))
        eps_hat = -np.sqrt(1 - abar[t]) * s            # eq-epsilon-score-conversion
        x_hat = (x - np.sqrt(1 - abar[t]) * eps_hat) / np.sqrt(abar[t])
        bt2 = (1 - abar[t - 1]) / (1 - abar[t]) * (1 - alpha[t])
        c = np.sqrt(max(1 - abar[t - 1] - eta ** 2 * bt2, 0.0))
        z = rng.standard_normal(x.shape)
        x = (np.sqrt(abar[t - 1]) * x_hat           # denoise + rescale
             + c * eps_hat + eta * np.sqrt(bt2) * z)  # re-noise
        if after_step is not None:
            x = after_step(x, t - 1)
    return x


def report(name: str, x: np.ndarray) -> None:
    off = np.abs(np.hypot(x[:, 0], x[:, 1] + 1) - 2.5)  # dist. to arc
    m, s = x.mean(0), x.std(0)
    print(f"{name:22s} mean ({m[0]:+.3f}, {m[1]:+.3f}) "
          f"std ({s[0]:.3f}, {s[1]:.3f}) off-arc {off.mean():.3f}")
```

### Step 3: unconditional sampling

```{.python}
# (3) Unconditional sampling, DDPM (eta = 1) and DDIM (eta = 0).
B = 4000
x_T = lambda: rng.standard_normal((B, 2))              # noqa: E731
report("prior (direct samples)", gmm_sample(B, prior))
report("DDPM, exact score", reverse(x_T(), T, prior, eta=1.0))
report("DDIM, exact score", reverse(x_T(), T, prior, eta=0.0))
```

Output:

```{.text}
prior (direct samples) mean (-0.010, +0.874) std (1.586, 0.556) off-arc 0.055
DDPM, exact score      mean (-0.027, +0.877) std (1.585, 0.551) off-arc 0.048
DDIM, exact score      mean (-0.016, +0.855) std (1.604, 0.563) off-arc 0.051
```

DDPM and DDIM both reproduce the prior to about $0.02$, as
@prp-ddim-marginal says every $\eta$ should. Their samples sit slightly
closer to the arc than true samples (off-arc $0.048$ and $0.051$ against
$0.055$); this is discretisation error of a 200-step chain, and with
$T = 1000$ (all $\beta_t$ divided by five) the values become $0.054$ and
$0.056$.

### Step 4: posterior sampling and ILVR

We observe the first coordinate, $y = x_{0,1} + n$ with $y = 1.2$ and
$\sigma_{n} = 0.05$.

```{.python}
# (4) Observe the first coordinate: y = x_{0,1} + n, n ~ N(0, 0.05^2).
A, y, var_n = np.array([[1.0, 0.0]]), np.array([1.2]), 0.05 ** 2
post = condition(prior, A, y, var_n)
report("exact posterior", gmm_sample(B, post))
# p(x_t | y) is the posterior pushed through the forward kernel, so
# reverse(..., post) uses grad log p(x_t) + grad log p(y | x_t) exactly.
report("conditional score", reverse(x_T(), T, post))

# ILVR (eq-ilvr): phi = projection onto the first coordinate.
y_ref = np.array([1.2, -0.5])                  # only phi(y_ref) is used


def ilvr(x: np.ndarray, t: int) -> np.ndarray:
    z = rng.standard_normal(x.shape)
    y_t = np.sqrt(abar[t]) * y_ref + np.sqrt(1 - abar[t]) * z
    return np.stack([y_t[:, 0], x[:, 1]], 1)   # phi(y_t) + (I - phi)(x')


report("ILVR", reverse(x_T(), T, prior, after_step=ilvr))
report("exact posterior, n = 0", gmm_sample(B, condition(prior, A, y,
                                                          1e-8)))
```

Output:

```{.text}
exact posterior        mean (+1.196, +1.227) std (0.050, 0.076) off-arc 0.057
conditional score      mean (+1.197, +1.227) std (0.043, 0.066) off-arc 0.050
ILVR                   mean (+1.200, +1.197) std (0.000, 0.093) off-arc 0.061
exact posterior, n = 0 mean (+1.200, +1.228) std (0.000, 0.073) off-arc 0.056
```

1. **The conditional score gives the posterior.** The exact
   $\nabla\log p(x_t \mid y)$ reproduces the posterior
   mean to three decimals; its spread is about $13\%$ too small, the same
   discretisation effect as in step 3 (with $T = 1000$ the standard
   deviations are $0.048$ and $0.074$, against $0.051$ and $0.076$).
2. **ILVR satisfies the constraint exactly**: $x_1 = 1.2$ with zero spread,
   as fact (i) of @sec-guidance promised.
3. **ILVR is not exact posterior sampling.** Against the noise-free
   posterior (last line), the free coordinate has mean $1.197$ instead of
   $1.228$ and standard deviation $0.093$ instead of $0.073$, and this gap
   does *not* shrink with $T$ ($1.198$ and $0.095$ at $T = 1000$). A
   plausible reading: @eq-ilvr overwrites $x_1$ at every level with an
   *independently* noised copy of the reference, so the sequence is not a
   path of the forward process conditioned on $y$.

### Step 5: SDEdit, faithfulness against realism

The guide $x^{g} = (0.4, 0.2)$ lies inside the crescent's arc,
about $1.2$ away from the data.

```{.python}
# (5) SDEdit from an off-manifold guide: faithfulness vs realism.
guide = np.array([0.4, 0.2])
for t0 in [10, 40, 120]:
    z = rng.standard_normal((B, 2))
    x_t0 = np.sqrt(abar[t0]) * guide + np.sqrt(1 - abar[t0]) * z
    out = reverse(x_t0, t0, prior)
    off = np.abs(np.hypot(out[:, 0], out[:, 1] + 1) - 2.5).mean()
    dist = np.linalg.norm(out - guide, axis=1).mean()
    print(f"t0 = {t0:3d}: SNR {abar[t0] / (1 - abar[t0]):6.2f}, "
          f"dist to guide {dist:.3f}, off-arc {off:.3f}")

# eq-sdedit-posterior: from ONE fixed x_{t0}, the output is
# distributed as p(x_0 | x_{t0}).
t0 = 40
z = rng.standard_normal(2)
x_t0 = np.sqrt(abar[t0]) * guide + np.sqrt(1 - abar[t0]) * z
report("SDEdit from one x_t0", reverse(np.tile(x_t0, (B, 1)), t0, prior))
exact = condition(prior, np.sqrt(abar[t0]) * np.eye(2), x_t0,
                  1 - abar[t0])
report("exact p(x_0 | x_t0)", gmm_sample(B, exact))
```

Output:

```{.text}
t0 =  10: SNR  68.18, dist to guide 0.990, off-arc 0.260
t0 =  40: SNR   3.69, dist to guide 1.467, off-arc 0.046
t0 = 120: SNR   0.13, dist to guide 1.773, off-arc 0.049
SDEdit from one x_t0   mean (+1.868, +0.530) std (0.430, 0.440) off-arc 0.044
exact p(x_0 | x_t0)    mean (+1.851, +0.540) std (0.452, 0.454) off-arc 0.052
```

At $t_0 = 10$ (SNR $68$) the output stays closest to the guide but is five
times further from the arc than real samples: faithful and unrealistic. At
$t_0 = 40$ (SNR $3.7$) it is already as realistic as the prior, and at
$t_0 = 120$ (SNR $0.13$) it is close to an unconditional sample. The last
two lines check @eq-sdedit-posterior directly: chains started from one
fixed $x_{t_0}$ match exact samples of
$p(x_0 \mid x_{t_0})$ from case (c), so SDEdit with an
exact reverse chain is posterior sampling.


## Connections and further reading

- **Within the book.** The sampler is @eq-ddim-step of @sec-ddim, the
  noise-to-score conversion is @eq-epsilon-score-conversion, and the
  geometry the samplers must respect is
  [Why Diffusion Models](ch08.qmd). Latent diffusion has no chapter of its
  own in this book; it enters here, as the space in which the text-conditioned
  model runs.
- **Conditional training.** SR3 [@saharia2022sr3] concatenates the
  condition; latent diffusion [@rombach2022ldm] moves the process into a
  learned latent space and brings the condition in through cross-attention;
  eDiff-I [@balaji2022ediffi] splits the noise schedule between expert
  denoisers; DALL-E 2 [@ramesh2022dalle2] and Sora [@brooks2024sora]
  (@fig-sora) are the systems the lecture ends on.
- **Guidance.** SDEdit [@meng2022sdedit] conditions through the initial
  point and ILVR [@choi2021ilvr] at every step. Classifier-free guidance,
  which the lecture does not reach, is the other member of this family and
  is treated where the course returns to it.
- **Inverse problems.** The manifold reading of the reverse step
  [@chung2022mcg] and diffusion posterior sampling [@chung2023dps] are the
  continuation of @sec-guidance.
